c1-61.title: Hard questions in society
c1-61.story: Anna's ethics class held its monthly debate on Friday, and the list of topics looked intimidating. Lisa drew [[euthanasia]], so she had to argue whether doctors should ever help terminally ill patients end their lives. Max and Ira were paired on abortion, with Max presenting the [[pro-choice]] position and Ira the [[pro-life]] one, even though neither of them fully agreed with their assigned side. Anna's own topic was prejudice. She showed how [[homophobia]] and [[antisemitism]] often grow from the same fear of people seen as different, and she compared them with [[apartheid]] in South Africa, where racism was written into law. Then she played a short documentary clip about a young man who had joined an [[extremist]] group at sixteen. He described how he had shaved his head, become a [[skinhead]], and spent years believing that hatred made him strong. What changed him, he said, was a teacher who simply kept talking to him. When the debate ended, nobody had won every argument, but the teacher pointed out that they had disagreed for an hour without a single insult. Max said that might be the hardest skill of all.

c1-62.title: Election night
c1-62.story: Anna's politics seminar spent election night watching results from three countries at once. Max was tracking an American race, where a first-time candidate had come out of nowhere to win the [[primaries]] and was now challenging a long-serving [[congressman]] for his seat. "If she wins, she'll be the first [[congresswoman]] from that district," Max said, refreshing the map. Lisa followed Britain, reminding everyone that a [[Tory]] is simply a member of the country's main conservative party, while Ira covered a smaller European country where a veteran [[social democrat]] hoped to become [[premier]]. Anna's job was to compare the campaigns, and she noticed that every winner had a short, clear [[agenda]] focused on housing and prices. Around midnight, Ira's candidate gave a victory speech, claiming a strong [[mandate]] for change. Sofia, who had brought snacks, asked whether a [[liberal]] could ever win in a rural region like the one Max was watching. By two in the morning they had the answer: the newcomer had won by four hundred votes. "The [[electorate]] clearly wanted someone new," Anna wrote in her notes, just before falling asleep on the sofa.

c1-63.title: Inside the government
c1-63.story: Anna needed a student visa for a summer program abroad, so on Monday morning she went to the [[consulate]] with a folder full of documents. The [[bureaucrat]] at the window studied her papers for a long time and then asked for three more forms. While she waited, she read the news on her phone: the president had used his [[veto]] to block a new tax law, and the opposition was already talking about [[impeachment]]. The man in an expensive suit next to her turned out to be a [[lobbyist]] for an energy company, and he complained loudly that he was missing a press [[briefing]] at the ministry. To pass the time, Anna opened her history textbook, which described how a Roman [[prefect]] ruled a province on behalf of the emperor. She smiled at the thought that the emperor's officials had probably demanded extra forms too. Finally, the [[consul]] himself came out, apologized for the delay, and signed her application. He mentioned that English had become the [[de facto]] working language of the program's [[secretariat]], so she wouldn't need any other language. Anna walked out into the sunshine, holding her visa like a trophy.

c1-64.title: Big political ideas
c1-64.story: The night before her history exam, Anna sat at the kitchen table with Max and her grandfather, trying to make sense of three centuries of political ideas. Grandpa explained [[Marxism]] better than the textbook did: the theory predicted that the [[proletariat]], the working class, would eventually rise up against the factory owners. "It also claimed that [[capitalism]] would destroy itself," Grandpa said, "and yet here we are, still shopping online." Max summarized [[liberalism]] as the belief that individual freedom should come first, while Anna wrote a note on how [[nationalism]] had helped both to build countries and to start wars. Then they argued about an [[anarchist]] Max had read about, who wanted to abolish every government on earth. "So is a [[loyalist]] the opposite?" Anna asked. "Not exactly," Grandpa replied, "that's someone who stays faithful to a king or a state when others rebel." Finally, they reviewed how the Eastern [[bloc]] had collapsed and why so many countries signed a defense [[pact]] afterward. Anna passed the exam the next day, and she brought Grandpa a cake to say thank you.

c1-65.title: In the courtroom
c1-65.story: On Sunday evening, Anna and her dad finally watched the last episode of a British legal drama they had been following for weeks. The hero was a young [[barrister]] who had agreed to defend a struggling farmer [[pro bono]], because the man could not afford a lawyer. The farmer was accused of setting fire to a neighbor's barn, and the prosecution kept pointing out that he had failed a [[polygraph]] test. "Those machines aren't even accepted as evidence in most courts," Dad muttered. In the key scene, the [[coroner]] testified that the night guard found in the barn had died of a heart attack hours before the fire started, which changed everything. Because the case involved a new kind of insurance contract, it had been sent to a special [[tribunal]], and the barrister argued that its decision would set a [[precedent]] for thousands of farmers. When the [[verdict]] of not guilty was finally read, Anna actually cheered at the screen. Then the credits rolled, followed by a [[disclaimer]] saying that all the characters and events were fictional. "Good," said Dad, "because I'd hate to think a real court took that long."

c1-66.title: The crime boss
c1-66.story: Max had been writing a crime thriller all semester, and on Thursday he finally let Anna read the first draft. The villain ran a powerful drug [[cartel]] and had built an international [[syndicate]] with partners as far away as the [[yakuza]] in Tokyo. The detective, a tired woman named Vera, had spent ten years building a thick [[dossier]] on him, but she had never found enough evidence for an arrest. Everything changed after the [[kidnapping]] of a judge's son, which Vera suspected was part of an old [[vendetta]] between the villain and the judge's family. On the [[pretext]] of fixing a broken internet connection, she got inside the villain's mansion and discovered records linking him to human [[trafficking]] across three countries. Anna loved the tension, but she laughed at a scene in which the police raided a suspect's apartment and found nothing more dangerous than an old [[bong]] under the bed. "That's supposed to be funny," Max said defensively. "It is," Anna admitted, "but maybe Vera shouldn't solve the whole case in one chapter." Max sighed, opened his laptop, and started rewriting chapter two.

c1-67.title: A dangerous mind
c1-67.story: Ira had just started a criminal psychology course, and over coffee she told Anna and Lisa that most crime movies get almost everything wrong. In films, the villain is always a brilliant [[psychopath]] with a chilling smile, but her professor said real cases are usually far less glamorous. He explained that a [[sociopath]], by contrast, tends to be impulsive and quick to anger rather than coldly calculating. Another myth is the villain pressing a cloth soaked in [[chloroform]] over someone's face, since in reality it takes minutes to work and could easily kill the victim. The lecture Ira found most useful was about everyday dangers like [[stalking]], which often begins with someone constantly checking a person's social media and turning up wherever they go. Her professor stressed that an [[abuser]] is usually someone the victim already knows, and that a [[pedophile]] may pretend to be a friendly teenager online to gain a child's trust. The class had even discussed why [[incest]] is a crime in almost every legal system, and why [[cannibalism]], which shocks us so deeply, actually occurs among some animals when food runs out. Lisa admitted that after so many thrillers, she sometimes felt a touch of [[paranoia]] when walking home alone at night. Ira smiled and said the course had actually made her calmer, because knowing the real warning signs is far better than being afraid of everything.

c1-68.title: An army on the move
c1-68.story: On Saturday, Anna took her little brother Taras to the military history museum, where their grandfather volunteers as a guide. The first hall was devoted to ancient Rome, and Grandpa explained that a [[centurion]] commanded about a hundred soldiers and fought in the front row himself. In the next room, Taras pressed his nose against a model of an enormous [[armada]] of wooden warships sailing toward an enemy coast. Grandpa, who had served in the navy for thirty years, admitted that he had never become an [[admiral]], but he joked that he had once brought one a cup of coffee. He showed them a photo of himself as an eighteen-year-old [[cadet]], so thin that his uniform looked two sizes too big. Back then, every new [[recruit]] had to practice the same difficult [[maneuver]] for bringing a ship into port during a storm. The last hall told the story of a [[battalion]] that had protected a [[convoy]] of trucks carrying food to a city under siege, and a quiet display honored the [[heroism]] of the drivers. Next to it, a map showed how several countries built up a nuclear [[arsenal]] during the Cold War. On the way home, Taras announced that he was going to join the navy, and Grandpa promised to teach him sailor's knots first.
